question: Does the EU AI Act apply to AI systems or AI models or both?
candidate_answer: The EU AI Act's core regime governs AI systems, defined in Article 3(1) and brought within scope by Article 2, through the risk-based tiers (prohibited practices under Article 5, high-risk systems under Article 6, and limited-risk transparency duties under Article 50). General-purpose AI models are regulated separately under Chapter V (Articles 51 to 56), are defined in Article 3(63), and carry their own provider obligations with additional duties for models posing systemic risk. The Regulation therefore applies to both AI systems and general-purpose AI models under two parallel regimes.
reference_answer: The Regulation applies to both AI systems and, separately, general-purpose AI models. Under Article 2(1)(a), it covers providers placing on the market or putting into service AI systems, and providers placing on the market general-purpose AI models in the Union, regardless of where those providers are established or located. The remaining scope points in Article 2(1) (deployers, importers, distributors, product manufacturers, authorised representatives, affected persons) concern AI systems specifically, while general-purpose AI models are addressed separately through the dedicated obligations placed on their providers.

question: Which article of the EU AI Act governs human oversight measures?
candidate_answer: Article 14 governs human oversight measures for high-risk AI systems. It requires that such systems be designed and developed to enable natural persons to effectively oversee their operation, including understanding their capabilities and limitations, mitigating automation bias, interpreting outputs, and intervening or overriding decisions. Under Article 14(5), for remote biometric identification systems listed in Annex III(1)(a), no action or decision may be taken based on the system’s output unless it is verified by at least two competent individuals, except where Union or national law deems this disproportionate for law-enforcement or border-control purposes.
reference_answer: Human oversight of high-risk AI systems is governed by Article 14 of the EU AI Act. Such systems must be designed, including via human-machine interface tools, to be effectively overseen by natural persons while in use, with the aim of preventing or minimising risks to health, safety or fundamental rights. Oversight measures, commensurate with the system's risks and autonomy, must be built in by the provider before market placement and/or made implementable by the deployer. These measures must enable overseers to understand the system's capabilities and limitations, monitor its operation, guard against automation bias, correctly interpret outputs, decide not to use or to override/reverse outputs, and intervene or halt the system via a stop function.

question: What is the meaning and purpose of 'testing data' in the context of AI systems, and why is it important that it is not leaked during the training process?
candidate_answer: Testing data is defined in Article 3(32) as data used to provide an independent evaluation of the AI system, in order to confirm its expected performance before it is placed on the market or put into service. It must be kept separate from the training and validation data so that this evaluation is genuinely independent. If testing data leaks into the training process, the system is in effect assessed on data it has already seen, which inflates its apparent performance and defeats the purpose of the independent check that Article 10 requires for the datasets of a high-risk AI system.
reference_answer: Testing data is one of the training, validation and testing data sets referred to in Article 10(1), used to check a high-risk AI system against its intended purpose after training and validation (and, per Article 10(6), it is the sole such data set for systems not built by training AI models). Under Article 10(3), it must be relevant, sufficiently representative, to the best extent possible free of errors, and complete, with appropriate statistical properties for the persons or groups concerned. It must not be leaked into the training process because doing so destroys its independence: the system would then be evaluated on data it has already learned from, producing artificially inflated accuracy that masks real errors, biases or gaps and undermines the reliability of the whole compliance assessment.

question: What obligations, if any, does the EU AI Act set in place for AI systems that interact directly with natural persons? What exceptions, if any, apply?
candidate_answer: Limited risk, subject to transparency obligations. This obligation does not apply to AI systems authorised by law to detect, prevent, investigate or prosecute criminal offences, provided appropriate safeguards are in place, unless the system is available to the public to report crimes (Article 50(1)). Deployers of emotion recognition or biometric categorisation systems must inform exposed individuals (Article 50(3)), and deployers of deep fakes must disclose the artificial nature of the content (Article 50(4)), with exceptions for artistic, creative or satirical works and for AI-generated text subject to human editorial responsibility.
reference_answer: Article 50(1) requires providers of AI systems intended to interact directly with natural persons to design and develop them so those persons are informed they are interacting with an AI system. This obligation does not apply where it is obvious, from the perspective of a reasonably well-informed, observant and circumspect person, taking into account the circumstances and context of use, that they are dealing with an AI system. It also does not apply to AI systems authorised by law to detect, prevent, investigate or prosecute criminal offences, subject to appropriate safeguards for the rights and freedoms of third parties — unless such systems are available for the public to report a criminal offence, in which case the disclosure obligation still applies.

question: What are all the risk categories in the EU AI Act?
candidate_answer: The EU AI Act sets four risk tiers plus a separate regime for general-purpose AI models: unacceptable-risk practices are prohibited under Article 5; and high-risk systems are classified under Article 6 (an Annex I product safety component, or an Annex III use case) and carry the Chapter III Section 2 obligations. Limited-risk systems carry the Article 50 transparency duties, minimal-risk systems have no mandatory duties under the Act, and general-purpose AI models are governed separately under Articles 51 to 56, with added obligations under Article 55 for models classified as having systemic risk under Article 51.
reference_answer: The EU AI Act follows a four-tier, risk-based approach. Unacceptable-risk AI practices are prohibited outright under Article 5. High-risk AI systems, as defined in Article 6, cover AI used as a safety component of products (or the AI itself as a product) under the Annex I harmonisation legislation requiring third-party conformity assessment, as well as the use cases listed in Annex III; these must comply with the mandatory requirements of Title III. Limited-risk AI systems, such as chatbots or emotion-recognition and deepfake-generating systems, are subject only to the transparency obligations of Article 50. All remaining AI systems pose minimal or no risk and carry no mandatory obligations, though providers are encouraged to adhere to voluntary codes of conduct under Article 95.

question: Does "systemic risk" apply to AI systems or general purpose AI models or both?
candidate_answer: Systemic risk applies to general-purpose AI models, not to AI systems. Under Article 51(1), a general-purpose AI model is classified as a model with systemic risk where it has high impact capabilities evaluated on the basis of appropriate technical tools and methodologies, including indicators and benchmarks; under Article 51(2) a model is presumed to have high impact capabilities where the cumulative computation used for its training exceeds 10^25 floating point operations. The Commission may also designate a model on the basis of the Annex XIII criteria. A model classified as having systemic risk then carries the additional Article 55 obligations: model evaluation including adversarial testing, assessment and mitigation of systemic risks at Union level, serious-incident reporting, and adequate cybersecurity. The high-risk regime for AI systems under Articles 6 and Annex III is a separate classification and does not use the systemic-risk concept.
reference_answer: "Systemic risk" under the AI Act applies only to general-purpose AI models, not to AI systems. Article 51(1) classifies a general-purpose AI model as one with systemic risk if it has high-impact capabilities, evaluated using appropriate technical tools and methodologies, or if the Commission decides, ex officio or following a qualified alert from the scientific panel, that it has capabilities or impact equivalent to that threshold, having regard to the Annex XIII criteria. Article 51(2) adds a presumption of high-impact capability where training compute exceeds 10^25 FLOPs. This classification and its obligations attach to the model itself, not to any downstream AI system.

question: Under the EU AI Act, which specific AI systems are explicitly listed as high-risk because they make decisions in critical life- and health-related situations involving emergency calls and triage?
candidate_answer: Under Annex III point 5(d), AI systems intended to be used for dispatching or prioritising in dispatching emergency first-response services, or for triage of emergency medical-service patients (including by fire brigades and medical aid), are explicitly listed as high-risk. They fall within the 'essential private and public services' category of the eight Annex III high-risk use cases and are classified as high-risk through the Annex III route of Article 6(2), which treats any system falling within a listed use case as high-risk. That classification triggers the Chapter III Section 2 obligations for high-risk systems.

This point falls under Annex III area 5, covering access to and enjoyment of essential private and public services and benefits, within the high-risk classification framework of Article 6(2).

question: Is an AI system used to structure or deduplicate information for a use case listed in Annex III considered high-risk?
candidate_answer: Under Article 6(3), an Annex III system is not high-risk where it poses no significant risk of harm and meets one of four conditions: it performs a narrow procedural task, it improves the result of a previously completed human activity, it detects decision-making patterns or deviations without replacing or influencing the human assessment, or it performs a preparatory task. Under Article 6(3), this exception never applies where the system profiles natural persons. The provider must document the assessment before placing the system on the market and register it under Article 49(2).
reference_answer: No. Structuring or deduplicating information for an Annex III use case is a narrow procedural task within the meaning of Article 6(3), first subparagraph, point (a), so the system benefits from the derogation and is not high-risk, provided it does not otherwise pose a significant risk of harm to health, safety or fundamental rights, including by not materially influencing decision-making outcomes. Notwithstanding this, the system remains high-risk if it performs profiling of natural persons. The provider must still document this non-high-risk assessment under Article 6(4) before placing the system on the market or putting it into service, and remains subject to the registration obligation in Article 49(2).

question: Consider the situation in which a market surveillance authority (MSA) determines that an AI system, originally classified as non-high-risk by the provider, is in fact high-risk. Does the provider need to recall and suspend the use of the system without undue delay, or does the MSA provide a timeframe within which the provider can take corrective actions? Or does this depend on the gravity of the situation?
candidate_answer: The provider does not need to recall or suspend the system without undue delay; instead, the market surveillance authority (MSA) must first carry out an evaluation under Article 80 and, if misclassification is confirmed, require corrective actions within a period prescribed by the authority, proportionate to the risk. This applies specifically where the system was classified as non-high-risk under Article 6(3) but is found to be high-risk, triggering the MSA’s power to mandate compliance under Article 80(2). The authority may impose provisional measures under Article 79(5) only if the provider fails to act within the given timeframe. The procedure integrates with Regulation (EU) 2019/1020, ensuring proportionality and Union-wide coordination via the safeguard procedure in Article 81.
reference_answer: Under Article 80(2), once the MSA finds the system is actually high-risk, it does not impose an automatic duty to recall or suspend the system without undue delay. Instead, it requires the provider to take all necessary actions to bring the system into compliance and to take appropriate corrective action within a period that the MSA itself prescribes. Article 80(4) confirms the provider must act within that period; only failure to comply in time triggers fines under Article 99, with Article 80(6) then applying the Article 79(5)-(9) procedure. The Regulation sets this fixed authority-set-period mechanism regardless of the gravity of the situation.

question: Under the EU AI Act, what presumption applies when a high-risk AI system is trained and tested on data that reflects the specific geographical, behavioural, contextual or functional setting in which it is intended to be used?
candidate_answer: Article 42(1) of the EU AI Act provides a presumption of conformity for high-risk AI systems trained and tested on data that reflects the specific geographical, behavioural, contextual, or functional setting in which they are intended to be used. Such systems are presumed to comply with the data-governance requirements of Article 10(4), which mandates that training, validation, and testing datasets be representative and account for the relevant characteristics of the intended use environment. This presumption simplifies compliance with data governance obligations where the data aligns with the system’s deployment context.

This presumption applies only to the extent required by the intended purpose. It does not exempt the provider from the system's other Article 10 obligations, such as data governance practices and bias examination and mitigation under Article 10(2), points (f) and (g).

question: When registering a high-risk AI system in the EU database under the EU AI Act, what specific information must the provider submit? List the required items.
candidate_answer: Providers must submit the information listed in Section A of Annex VIII to register a high-risk AI system in the EU database under Article 49. This includes the provider’s name, address and contact details; the authorised representative’s details if applicable; the AI system’s trade name and identification reference; a description of its intended purpose, components and functions; a concise description of its inputs and operating logic; the system’s status; the notified body’s certificate details and scanned copy if applicable; the Member States where the system is available; and the electronic instructions for use and EU declaration of conformity. The Commission manages the EU database under Article 71, ensuring it is publicly accessible, machine-readable and searchable, except for restricted sections. For high-risk systems in law enforcement, migration, asylum and border control, registration is in a secure non-public section with limited data disclosure under Article 49(4).
reference_answer: Under Article 49(4), for high-risk AI systems listed in points 1, 6 and 7 of Annex III used in law enforcement, migration, asylum or border control management, registration is made only in a secure, non-public section of the EU database referred to in Article 71. The provider must submit only the following: Annex VIII Section A, points 1 to 10, excluding points 6, 8 and 9; Section B, points 1 to 5, and points 8 and 9; Section C, points 1 to 3; and Annex IX, points 1, 2, 3 and 5. Access to this restricted section is limited to the Commission and the national authorities referred to in Article 74(8).

question: Under Article 10(5) of the EU AI Act, when may a provider of a high-risk AI system process special categories of personal data for bias detection and correction, and what key safeguards/conditions must be met?
candidate_answer: Under Article 10(5), a provider of a high-risk AI system may exceptionally process special categories of personal data only to the extent strictly necessary to ensure bias detection and correction, subject to appropriate safeguards. Article 10(5) requires all of the following: the bias work cannot be done with other data, including synthetic or anonymised data (a); technical limits on re-use plus state-of-the-art security and pseudonymisation (b); strict, documented access controls to prevent misuse (c); no transmission or transfer to other parties (d); deletion once the bias is corrected or the retention period ends, whichever is first (e); and records of processing documenting why it was strictly necessary (f).

question: Under the EU AI Act, what specific information must a provider/prospective provider submit (and keep up to date) regarding testing of a high-risk AI system in real-world conditions outside an AI regulatory sandbox?
candidate_answer: A provider must submit and keep up to date a specific sandbox plan agreed with the competent authority under Article 57(5), detailing the development, training, testing, and validation of the high-risk AI system in real-world conditions outside the sandbox. Competent authorities must provide guidance, supervision, and support to identify and mitigate risks to fundamental rights, health, and safety under Article 57(6). The provider may also request a written proof of successful sandbox activities and an exit report from the competent authority, which can be used to demonstrate compliance during conformity assessment or market surveillance under Article 57(7). These documents must reflect the system’s real-world testing outcomes and risk mitigation measures.
reference_answer: Before testing in real-world conditions, the provider or prospective provider must draw up a real-world testing plan and submit it to the market surveillance authority of the Member State where testing occurs (Article 60(4)(a)). It must also register the testing with a Union-wide unique single identification number. question:

- the repurposed AI system is still high-risk due to reversibility of training into the original system
- the repurposed AI system is no longer high-risk but it must be reported in the EU database
- the repurposed AI system is no longer high-risk and there is no need to report it in the EU database
candidate_answer: The repurposed AI system is no longer high-risk and there is no need to report it in the EU database. Under Article 6(3), an AI system listed in Annex III is not considered high-risk if it no longer poses a significant risk of harm and fulfils one of the four conditions: it performs a narrow procedural task, improves a previously completed human activity, detects decision-making patterns without replacing human assessment, or performs a preparatory task. Since the system is repurposed to a use case not in Annex III, it no longer falls under the high-risk classification. Article 71 does not require registration in the EU database for systems that are no longer high-risk.
reference_answer: The repurposed system is no longer high-risk, and there is no need to report it in the EU database. Under Article 6(2), high-risk classification attaches to the AI system by reference to Annex III use cases (or, under Article 6(1), Annex I safety-component coverage) — i.e., to its intended purpose, not to the underlying model or its training. Reversibility of training into the original system is irrelevant. Once the provider redirects the system to a use case outside both Annex III and Annex I, neither limb of Article 6 is met, so the system exits the high-risk category entirely. Since it is not high-risk, the registration duty under Article 49 and the EU database under Article 71 do not apply.

question: We have a phone system where the caller can press 1 if they consent to the call being recorded, 2 if they do not. We wish to replace this with an NLP system that understands a voice reply like "Yes", "Sure", "Please no", etc. Would such a system be considered high-risk? It's for our clinic.
candidate_answer: Not high-risk. An NLP system that interprets voice replies for call recording consent is not listed in Annex III and does not qualify as a safety component of a medical device under Article 6(1), so it is not high-risk. The system does not engage in any of the eight prohibited practices under Article 5, such as emotion recognition in educational or workplace settings, biometric categorisation, or social scoring. As a limited-risk system, it falls under the transparency obligations of Article 50, requiring the provider to inform individuals they are interacting with an AI system.
reference_answer: No, this system would not be high-risk under Article 6(2). Annex III(1)(b)-(c) covers AI used for biometric categorisation or emotion recognition, but this system merely interprets the literal semantic content of a spoken reply (yes/no) to determine consent, not any emotional or sensitive/protected attribute inferred from voice, so it falls outside that category. It also does not fall under Annex III(5)(a), since that provision concerns evaluating eligibility for essential public assistance benefits and services, including healthcare, not capturing consent to call recording. Since no Annex III area applies, the system is not high-risk, regardless of the clinic context.

question: Does the AI Act prohibit or classifies as high-risk the use of AI in drones? Can I use AI in a drone to find who's around in town? And what if it's just a toy drone? And what about toy drones used for other applications?
candidate_answer: Prohibited only where a drone uses real-time remote biometric identification in publicly accessible spaces for law enforcement purposes, which is banned under Article 5(1)(h) subject to narrow exceptions for search and rescue, imminent terrorist threats, or locating suspects of serious crimes listed in Annex II. Otherwise, AI in drones is not categorically prohibited and may be high-risk depending on its use. High-risk classification arises under Article 6(2) if the AI system falls within an Annex III use case, such as migration and border control (Annex III.7), including risk assessment of individuals at borders or assisting in asylum applications. For non-prohibited uses, including toy drones, the system is not high-risk unless it performs a safety function in a product covered by Annex I legislation (e.g., machinery or toys requiring third-party conformity assessment), otherwise it is limited risk and subject to transparency obligations under Article 50(1) if interacting with natural persons.
reference_answer: The AI Act does not prohibit or classify drones as such as high-risk; under Article 6, classification depends on the AI system's intended use, not the device carrying it. Using a drone's AI to identify who is present in town is remote biometric identification, high-risk under Annex III(1)(a), since it identifies individuals rather than merely verifying a single claimed identity (the verification exclusion doesn't apply). A toy drone is treated no differently — being a toy does not exempt the system, so this same use remains high-risk. A toy drone used for another application is high-risk only if that application matches an Annex III use case, or is a safety component requiring third-party conformity assessment under Article 6(1).

question: Article 9 of the AI Act lists the five categories of harm that map to AI systems with: no risk, limited risk, high-risk, systemic risk, prohibited. What are the five categories and how do they map to the five risk levels?
candidate_answer: Prohibited. Article 5 bans eight specific AI practices: subliminal or manipulative techniques causing significant harm, exploitation of vulnerabilities based on age, disability, or socio-economic situation, social scoring of natural persons, individual criminal risk assessment based solely on profiling, untargeted scraping of facial images from the internet or CCTV, emotion recognition in workplaces or educational institutions (except for medical or safety reasons), biometric categorisation inferring sensitive attributes (race, political opinions, trade union membership, religious or philosophical beliefs, sex life, sexual orientation), and real-time remote biometric identification in publicly accessible spaces by law enforcement (with narrow exceptions). These practices are categorically prohibited under Article 5 and do not map to other risk levels. The EU AI Act establishes four risk tiers, prohibited, high-risk, limited risk, and minimal risk, alongside a separate regime for general-purpose AI models under Articles 51 to 56.The prohibited category corresponds to the practices outlined in Article 5, high-risk applies to systems in Annex III (subject to strict compliance obligations), limited risk includes systems requiring transparency obligations under Article 50, and minimal risk encompasses all other AI systems with no specific obligations.
reference_answer: No. Article 9 does not list five categories of harm mapped to risk tiers; it solely requires providers of high-risk AI systems to establish, implement, document and maintain a continuous, iterative risk management system throughout the system's lifecycle. That system comprises four steps: identification and analysis of known and reasonably foreseeable risks to health, safety or fundamental rights; estimation and evaluation of risks arising from intended use and reasonably foreseeable misuse; evaluation of further risks identified via post-market monitoring data; and adoption of targeted risk management measures addressing the risks found. The Act's prohibited/high-risk/limited-risk/minimal-risk/systemic-risk architecture instead derives from other provisions, such as Articles 5, 6, 50 and 51.

question: We deployed a high-risk AI system in our company. We have a use in mind that is outside the intended use and our legal team say such a use is definitely no risk (no Annex I nor III apply). Can we just go ahead with the new use and do we need to keep logs for it?
candidate_answer: Not high-risk under Annex I or Annex III for the new use, provided the new use falls outside both the safety component criteria of Annex I legislation and the listed high-risk use cases in Annex III. Article 6 establishes the two routes for high-risk classification: one via safety components of products under Annex I (such as medical devices requiring third-party conformity assessment), and another via specific use cases in Annex III (such as biometric identification, critical infrastructure, or education). Since the legal team confirms neither route applies, the system is not high-risk for this new use. However, Article 12 still requires deployers to ensure automatic logging of the system’s operation and use, regardless of risk level, to enable monitoring and traceability.
reference_answer: No. Under Article 26(1), deployers must use a high-risk AI system in accordance with its instructions for use; deploying it for a purpose outside that intended use breaches this obligation, regardless of whether the new use, viewed in isolation, would independently qualify as high-risk under Annex III. The system's high-risk classification attaches to it as placed on the market, so a deployer cannot unilaterally reassess risk use-by-use to sidestep Article 26. Logging duties are unaffected: under Article 26(6), deployers must still keep the automatically generated logs, to the extent under their control, for at least six months, irrespective of which use generated them.

question: Is an AI that transcribes doctor-patient conversations prohibited? Or is it high-risk as per the use cases of Annex III of the AI Act?
candidate_answer: Not prohibited and not high-risk unless the system is a safety component of a medical device requiring third-party conformity assessment under Annex I legislation, in which case it is high-risk under Article 6(1). Mere transcription of doctor-patient conversations is none of the eight prohibited practices in Article 5, including social scoring, emotion recognition, or biometric categorisation, and is not listed in Annex III as a high-risk use case. Absent integration into a regulated medical device, the system is limited risk, subject primarily to the Article 50 transparency obligation requiring providers to inform patients they are interacting with an AI system. The determining factor is whether the AI forms part of a medical device governed by MDR or IVDR that requires notified-body assessment.
reference_answer: No to both. Transcribing doctor-patient conversations is not among the prohibited practices listed in Article 5. It also does not qualify as high-risk under Annex III: even if used in a context otherwise touching an Annex III area, transcription is a narrow procedural task within the meaning of Article 6(3), first subparagraph, point (a), so the derogation removes it from high-risk classification. question: As a deployer, do I need to keep logs if I use a powerful LLM (surpassing the FLOPs threshold) for estimating whether customer payment confirmations are received via email?
candidate_answer: No, a deployer is not required to keep logs solely because the general-purpose AI model used exceeds the 10^25 FLOPs threshold for systemic risk. The record-keeping and logging obligation under Article 12 applies only to providers of high-risk AI systems, not to deployers, unless the deployer becomes a provider by putting their name or trademark on the system, making a substantial modification, or changing its intended purpose under Article 25(1). Systemic risk classification under Article 51 triggers enhanced provider obligations, including detailed technical documentation and model evaluation, but these do not extend to deployers who do not assume provider status. Deployers remain subject only to their own obligations under Article 26, which do not include logging.
reference_answer: No. The Article 26(6) log-keeping duty applies only to deployers of high-risk AI systems, i.e. systems falling within an Annex III use case (biometrics, critical infrastructure, education, employment, essential services, law enforcement, migration, or justice/democracy). Estimating whether customer payment confirmation emails were received is an ordinary administrative function that does not correspond to any Annex III area, so the system is not high-risk. The fact that the underlying LLM surpasses the FLOPs threshold is irrelevant here: that threshold governs classification of a general-purpose AI model as posing systemic risk under Article 51, a distinct regime from the Article 6/Annex III high-risk classification of AI systems. No Article 26(6) obligation therefore arises.

candidate_answer: The eight high-risk areas listed in Annex III are biometrics, critical infrastructure, education and vocational training, employment and worker management, essential private and public services, law enforcement, migration and asylum and border control, and administration of justice and democratic processes. Healthcare decision-making is included under the "essential private and public services" area, specifically where AI systems are used by or on behalf of public authorities to evaluate eligibility for healthcare services, grant or revoke benefits, or for emergency patient triage. Such systems are classified as high-risk under Article 6(2) if they fall within these defined use cases. Article 6(3) provides a carve-out where the system performs only a narrow procedural task, improves a previously completed human activity, detects decision-making patterns without replacing human assessment, or performs a preparatory task, unless it profiles natural persons.

question: Do providers of GPAI systems, even if not with systemic risk, have an obligation to extensively shield their models from adversarial attacks? What about specifically for adversarial images? What about specifically for prompt injection?
candidate_answer: Systemic risk applies to general-purpose AI models, not to AI systems. Under Article 51(1), a general-purpose AI model is classified as a model with systemic risk where it has high impact capabilities evaluated on the basis of appropriate technical tools and methodologies, including indicators and benchmarks; under Article 51(2) a model is presumed to have high impact capabilities where the cumulative computation used for its training exceeds 10^25 floating point operations. The Commission may also designate a model on the basis of the Annex XIII criteria. A model classified as having systemic risk then carries the additional Article 55 obligations: model evaluation including adversarial testing, assessment and mitigation of systemic risks at Union level, serious-incident reporting, and adequate cybersecurity. The high-risk regime for AI systems under Articles 6 and Annex III is a separate classification and does not use the systemic-risk concept.
reference_answer: No. The obligation to shield models from adversarial attacks does not apply to providers of general-purpose AI models generally; under Article 55(1)(a), it falls only on providers of general-purpose AI models with systemic risk, who must perform model evaluation using standardised protocols and tools reflecting the state of the art, including conducting and documenting adversarial testing to identify and mitigate systemic risks. Article 55(1)(a) does not single out adversarial images as a distinct category, referring only generically to adversarial testing. Prompt injection is likewise not separately addressed anywhere in Article 55, so no specific obligation regarding it exists, regardless of systemic-risk status.

question: Can law enforcement starts using a real-time remote biometric identification system without prior authorisation? If yes, how much time do they have to seek authorisation, and what happens if the authorisation is refused?
candidate_answer: No. The use of real-time remote biometric identification in publicly accessible spaces by law enforcement is prohibited under Article 5(1)(h), except where strictly necessary for one of three exhaustive objectives: the targeted search for victims of abduction, trafficking, or missing persons; prevention of a specific, substantial and imminent threat to life or physical safety; or the identification of a suspect of a serious criminal offence punishable by at least four years’ imprisonment. Even in those cases, prior judicial or administrative authorisation is required. If authorisation is refused, use of the system must stop immediately and all results discarded under Article 46(2).
reference_answer: Yes. Article 5(3) allows law enforcement to commence use of a 'real-time' remote biometric identification system in publicly accessible spaces without prior authorisation only in a duly justified situation of urgency. Authorisation from the competent judicial authority or an independent administrative authority whose decision is binding must nonetheless be requested without undue delay, and at the latest within 24 hours. If that authorisation is subsequently rejected, the use must be stopped with immediate effect, and all data, results and outputs generated from that use must be immediately discarded and deleted.

question: We developed a product listed in Annex I where an AI system is a safety component. We had the option to opt out of the third-party conformity assessment base case by using harmonized standards. Thus no third-party conformity assessment happened. This means we can skip the requirements of Chapter 3 Section 2 of the AI Act, right?
candidate_answer: Union harmonisation legislation list (Section A: New Legislative Framework, machinery, toys, radio equipment, medical devices, lifts, etc.; Section B: civil aviation, motor vehicles, marine equipment, rail, agricultural vehicles), AI safety-components of products covered here are classified high-risk under Article 6(1). Requires providers of high-risk AI to undergo a conformity assessment: internal-control procedure (Annex VI) for Annex-III systems where harmonised standards / common specifications are applied, otherwise notified-body procedure (Annex VII); for Annex-I products, Article 43(3) integrates the AI Act assessment into the sectoral third-party conformity-assessment procedure (for a medical device, the MDR notified-body assessment), one single procedure covering both regimes. Annex I route (Article 6(1)): the system is a safety component of, or is itself, a product covered by the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I AND that product must undergo a third-party conformity assessment under that sectoral legislation. Annex III route (Article 6(2)): the system falls within one of the use-cases listed under the eight AREAS of Annex III (an area is a numbered heading; a use case is a lettered entry under it). Article 6(3) derogation: an Annex III system is NOT high-risk where it poses no significant risk of harm and meets one of four conditions (a narrow procedural task; improving the result of a previously completed human activity; detecting decision-making patterns or deviations without replacing or influencing the human assessment; or a preparatory task), unless it profiles natural persons, in which case it is always high-risk; the provider must document this self-assessment before placing the system on the market.
reference_answer: No. Under Article 43(3), for high-risk AI systems covered by Union harmonisation legislation in Annex I Section A, the provider follows the conformity assessment procedure required by that sectoral legislation, but the Chapter III Section 2 requirements still apply to the system and form part of that very assessment. Opting out of third-party assessment under the sectoral act is permitted only if the manufacturer has also applied harmonised standards, or common specifications under Article 41, covering all the Section 2 requirements, not merely the sectoral ones. So the opt-out changes who performs the assessment, not whether Section 2's substantive requirements must be satisfied.
